_doc: English overlay for the v2 engine texts (docs/ENGINE_TEXTS.md): the same keys as data/engine_v2_params.json, texts and labels only; applied with merge_params / mergeParams on top of the params for locale en. No numbers except bands.list[].min: merge_params replaces arrays whole, so band ids and thresholds are an exact copy of params (verified by scripts/check_engine_texts.py). British spelling and “curly” quotes, as in frontend/src/app/core/i18n/en.ts; labels are bare nouns, articles and the possessive 's live in the templates.

texts.quiet: {dish} is louder than the drink ({fd} ↔ {fb}) — {drink} stays in the background
texts.w_boost: the drink's body is lighter than the dish ({wb} ↔ {wd}) — {helper} makes up for it (CMS)
texts.w_light: the drink's body is lighter than the dish ({wb} ↔ {wd})
texts.w_heavy: the drink is heavier than the dish ({wb} ↔ {wd})

texts.quiet_ok: {dish} is a touch louder than the drink ({fd} ↔ {fb}), but {drink} holds its own

texts.tannin: Tannins in the {cat_gen} bind the fat in the {fat_src} — astringency and richness cancel each other out (Peyrot des Gachons 2012)

texts.sweet: The {cat_gen}'s sweetness tames the heat of the {chili_gen} (CMS: “Spicy + sugar = no fire”)
texts.cold: Served cold ({temp} °C), the drink cools the receptors — the heat of the {chili_gen} feels softer (Nasrawi 1990)
texts.body: The {cat_gen}'s full body softens the heat of the {chili_gen}
texts.burn: {abv}% alcohol fires the same receptors as chilli — the pairing will run hotter than you'd like (Trevisani 2002)
texts.hop: {bitter_cap} amplifies the burn of the {chili_gen} (BA: “Hop Bitterness emphasizes Spiciness”)
texts.hop_abv: {ibu_abv} amplify the burn of the {chili_gen} (Sam Adams panel)
texts.tannin: The {cat_gen}'s tannins turn harsh with spicy food (Gaiser: “avoid tannin!”)
texts.carbonation: Strong carbonation irritates the same pain receptors as chilli (Garneau)
texts.heat_lover: Hops and alcohol play up the heat of the {chili_gen} — just the way you like it (BA: “Hop Bitterness emphasizes Spiciness”)

texts.contrast: Powerful hop bitterness{ibu_paren} cuts the cloying sweetness of {dish} — a contrast at equal loudness (BA)
texts.match: The {cat_gen}'s sweetness keeps pace with {dish} — the drink doesn't taste bitter (CMS: “Sweets need sweets”)
texts.near: The {cat_gen} is a touch less sweet than {dish} — well within range
texts.gap: {dish} is sweeter than the drink: next to it, {drink} will taste harsh and watery
texts.roast: Roasted notes in the {cat_gen} mirror the cocoa and balance the sweetness (BA: “Chocolate loves a dark beer”)
texts.roast_sweet: Roasted notes in the {cat_gen} balance the sweetness of {dish} (BA: “Roasted Malt balances Sweetness”)
texts.hot_contrast: Hot {drink} and the sweetness of {dish} make a classic contrast: astringency and bitterness cut the cloying edge (tea tradition; THAC)

texts.clean: The {cat_gen}'s acidity keeps up with the dish's tartness ({acid_src}) — the pairing tastes clean (CMS: “Acidity needs acidity”)
texts.flabby: The dish's tartness ({acid_src}) outweighs the {cat_gen}'s acidity — the drink will taste flat (“flabby”, CMS)
texts.vinegar_tannin: Vinegar in {dish} is the enemy of tannins: {drink} will taste harsh and flat

texts.forgive_bitter: {salt_src_cap} tames the bitterness{ibu_paren} — malt and fruit come through brighter (Breslin & Beauchamp)
texts.clean_acid: The {cat_gen}'s acidity balances the salt — the palate stays clean (CMS: “Acidity cuts saltiness”)
texts.clean_carb: The {cat_gen}'s bubbles rinse away the salt — the palate stays clean (NW Cider: “bubbles… cut… briny flavors”)
texts.snack: A salty snack is a classic: salt builds a thirst, bubbles and bitterness quench it
texts.tann: Salt makes firm tannins even harsher (Gaiser; disputed)

recommend.policy_note: Scores are honest and brand-blind. If drinks are within {window} pts of each other, the one from the Efes portfolio is listed first.

rules_summary.R1: The drink and the dish should be equally matched: light with light, rich with rich. If the drink is much louder than the dish, it drowns it out, and the pairing's other strengths barely count (BA, CMS).
rules_summary.R2: A rich dish calls for something that cuts the fat: tannins, bitterness, bubbles, acidity. Tannins work best — this has been measured in the lab (Peyrot des Gachons 2012).
rules_summary.R3: Heat is tamed by sweetness, milk protein and cold, and amplified by strong alcohol, intense bitterness and tannins (Trevisani 2002, Nolden 2019). For those who like it hot, the penalty is almost lifted.
rules_summary.R4: The drink shouldn't be drier than the dessert, or it will taste sour and thin (CMS). Exceptions: roasted malt with chocolate and sweets (BA), and hot tea or coffee — there the contrast does the work.
rules_summary.R5: The drink's acidity should be no lower than the dish's, or the drink tastes flat (CMS). Vinegar is especially unforgiving.
rules_summary.R6: Salt softens bitterness and astringency (Breslin, 1995 — measured) and gets along well with bubbles and acidity. Salty food with strong spirits is a minus.
rules_summary.R7: Without salt, umami makes bitter and tannic flavours harsher; with salt and acidity it opens up (Hanni, Papazian). Experts disagree here, so the weight is moderate.
rules_summary.R8: Tannins love protein and fat — think steak and red wine. With oily fish they turn metallic, with asparagus and spinach, bitter (CMS, WSET).
rules_summary.R9: Raw and delicate food wants something light, clean, not bitter and bubbly. Roast, a heavy body and high alcohol drown such dishes out.
rules_summary.R10: Caramel, toast and nuts in the drink echo the crust of fried and baked food (the Maillard reaction).
rules_summary.R11: Smoke with smoke: smoked and charcoal-grilled dishes go with smoky and roasty drinks.
rules_summary.R12: Shared aromas — citrus, bread, honey — build a “bridge” between the drink and the dish. This hasn't been tested scientifically, so its weight is small (level D).
rules_summary.R13: The best pairings work on two levels at once — contrast and harmony (BA) — and earn a small bonus for it.
rules_summary.R14: Bitter with bitter, or a sweet cocktail with a sweetish dish, is a minus: the flavours don't balance, they double up.
rules_summary.R15: A drink and a cuisine from the same region get a small bonus: classic cuisines grew up alongside their drinks.
rules_summary.R16: The occasion changes the pick: with dinner — light and fizzy, for an aperitif — a touch of bitterness and bubbles, in the heat — something refreshing, and “alcohol-free” is a strict filter.
rules_summary.R17: Your taste: how you feel about bitterness and sweetness, “I like it hot” and sensitivity to bitterness shift the score by a few points.
rules_summary.R18: Serving temperature changes how sweetness and bitterness come across. Switched off for now — we'll check it at a tasting.
rules_summary.R20: Pairings named outright in textbooks and guides (oysters and dry stout, steak and cabernet) get a small bonus and a “classic” badge. Each comes with a source and a quote.
